steps.scene: You've just passed your test. A friend offers to let you drive their car home after a party.

question.prompt: What must you check before you drive it?

options.text: Nothing — their insurance covers anyone who drives it
That the car is insured for you to drive
That it has enough fuel to get you home

question.explanation: Insurance covers named drivers, not the car itself. Check you're covered on their policy or your own before you drive.

steps.title: The legal minimum
steps.body: By law you need at least third-party insurance. It pays for damage and injury you cause to others — not for your own car.

question.prompt: What's the legal minimum insurance to drive on public roads?

options.text: Third party only
Fully comprehensive
Third party, fire and theft

question.explanation: Comprehensive cover also pays for your own car, but it's a choice. Third party is the minimum the law requires.

a.label: No valid MOT
a.body: Illegal to drive, and it may invalidate your insurance.

b.label: Driving to a booked MOT
b.body: Allowed if it's booked in advance and the car is otherwise roadworthy.

question.prompt: Your car needs an MOT. When may you drive it without a current certificate?

options.text: For a month after it runs out, as a grace period
On short local journeys only
When driving to a booked MOT appointment

question.explanation: There's no grace period. Book the test before the old certificate runs out.

steps.title: The registered keeper
steps.body: The keeper named on the V5C must keep it up to date. Tell DVLA when you move house, change your name or sell the car.

question.prompt: When should you update your vehicle registration certificate (V5C)?

options.text: Only when you sell the car
When you move house
Each time you renew your insurance

question.explanation: DVLA uses the V5C to reach you — for tax reminders, and for fines. An old address doesn't excuse you.

steps.scene: A police officer stops you and asks to see your insurance certificate. It's at home in a drawer.

options.text: You may be asked to show it at a police station within 7 days
You're committing an offence by not carrying it
Nothing — the police can't ask to see it

question.explanation: You don't have to carry your documents, but you must be able to produce them when asked.

steps.title: Your health and DVLA
steps.body: You must tell DVLA about any medical condition that could affect your driving — it's your duty, not your doctor's.

options.text: Only if your doctor says you must stop driving
Whenever you change your insurer
When a health condition could affect your driving

question.explanation: Some conditions, and some treatments, affect your fitness to drive. Telling DVLA is the law.

steps.wrongBelief: New drivers have the same 12-point limit as everyone else.

question.prompt: You passed your test a year ago. What happens if you reach 6 penalty points?

options.text: Nothing yet — the limit is 12 points
Your licence is revoked — you retake theory and practical tests
You must go on a speed awareness course

question.explanation: The rule covers your first two years after passing. Points from before you passed can count too.

steps.repairNote: Within 2 years of passing, 6 points revokes your licence. You go back to a provisional and must pass both tests again.
